Q: Is my noise function differentially private? Is flattening then reshaping correct? Or it breaks the image? A:

I do think it works, but I'm not quite sure if it is the correct approach. I'm applying noise to an image with more than 1 channel and using the flatten() function to calculate the sensitivity of the image more easily, later on i use the reshape() function to bring the image back to its original shape. Is this correct? Or should i apply the noise to each channel individually?

I don't think what you're doing is correct. I don't think that it is meaningful to ask what the sensitivity of a specific image is.

If you look at the definition of this on Wikipedia, you'll see that it requires you to calculate the mean with respect to the entire dataset, then with one furthest example removed. If you remove one image from a dataset of one image, then you have nothing left.

What you're calculating is how the mean of the dataset changes with one pixel removed. I don't think that's a meaningful quantity. In most cases, assuming an image contains average illumination, pixel values from 0-255, and at least one white or black pixel, you will find a sensitivity of approx 255 / np.prod(image1.shape) / 2.

Instead, I think you should compute sensitivity with respect to a dataset or batch. I don't think you can calculate the sensitivity of a single image.

I'm not sure I can provide specifics of how to do that - I can't make heads or tails of what the paper you linked is doing. They say that the sensitivity of ReLU is bounded in the range [0, 1], which I don't think is correct. So, I don't understand their argument that sensitivity is bounded in the range [0, 1.5].

The problem is: I've been adding the noise to the the flattened tensor and then reshaping it to its original form. But does reshaping it this way preserves its original space? For example, how do i guarantee that in input [[1, 2],[3, 4]] flatten -> [1, 2, 3, 4] reshaped output -> [[1,2],[3,4]] and not reshaped output [[4,3][2,1]].

This is controlled by the order parameter to flatten() and reshape(). By default this is 'C', for both flatten() and reshape(), which flattens into C order and reshapes assuming C order. It is guaranteed that .flatten().reshape(*original_shape) gives you back an equivalent array, regardless of the content of the array or its dtype. See docs for np.flatten() and np.reshape(). (The np.reshape() page has a particularly helpful example.)

Q: How do I insert primary and foreign key constraints and their columns of data into a large existing company database? A:

You definitely need to introduce Primary and Foreign keys!!!

The syntax to add a primary key on an existing table is as follows:

ALTER TABLE table_name
ADD CONSTRAINT constraint_name PRIMARY KEY (column1, column2, ... column_n);

To delete a constraint is as follows:

ALTER TABLE table_name
DROP CONSTRAINT constraint_name;

To disable:

ALTER TABLE table_name
DISABLE CONSTRAINT constraint_name;

if you need to do data cleansing the below will also come useful:

alter table t enable novalidate constraint uniq_a;

New records inserted will adhere to the constraints, but existing data will not be validated.

Q: How to execute or run .sql file inside stored procedure in oracle A:

I would suggest using Oracle Scheduler to execute your scripts with PL/SQL Packages Procs and use execute immediate when required for DDL.

Q: Average sum ignoring max or min A:

In SQL you simply just need to express the result, so ...

WITH D as(
SELECT  100.0 v FROM DUAL UNION
SELECT 102.0 FROM DUAL UNION
SELECT 103.0 FROM DUAL UNION
SELECT 105.0 FROM DUAL UNION
SELECT 107.0 FROM DUAL)
SELECT  avg(v)
FROM D
where (v < (select max(v) from D )
       and ((select max(v) from D )
            -(select max(v) from D where v != 
              (select max(v) from D ) ) > 1.5))
or
(v > (select min(v) from D )
       and ((select min(v) from D )
            +(select min(v) from D where v != 
              (select min(v) from D ) ) > 1.5))

... should do the trick!

But thinking ahead... the below version may also be useful ;)

  WITH D as(
    SELECT 1 PK, 100.0 v FROM DUAL UNION
    SELECT 1,102.0 FROM DUAL UNION
    SELECT 1,103.0 FROM DUAL UNION
    SELECT 1,105.0 FROM DUAL UNION
    SELECT 1,107.0 FROM DUAL)
    SELECT  PK,avg(v)
    FROM D
    where (v < (select max(v) from D group by PK)
           and ((select max(v) from D group by PK)
                -(select max(v) from D where v != 
                  (select max(v) from D group by PK) group by PK) > 1.5))
    or
    (v > (select min(v) from D group by PK)
           and ((select min(v) from D group by PK)
                +(select min(v) from D where v != 
                  (select min(v) from D group by PK) group by PK) > 1.5))
    
    GROUP BY PK

In real life though you would consider the execution plans of the above in a large dataset too (homework).

Q: Calculating a rolling count over a specified window A: 
Select  CallStart,
        CallDuration,
COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY trunc(CallStart,'mi') - 
         numtodsinterval(mod(to_char(CallStart,'mi'),15),'minute'))
as DropsIn15Minutes 
From    #Calls  C1

Q: How to display last 12 months of data in proper order in SQL A: 
select to_char(SCHEDULED_START_DT, 'MM-YYYY'), count(*)
from XYZ
where SCHEDULED_START_DT > TRUNC(ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, -11), 'MM')
group by to_char(SCHEDULED_START_DT, 'MM-YYYY') 
order by SCHEDULED_START_DT DESC;
